title: Joan of Arc on film
lead: Ten films on St Joan, from Méliès to Rivette, and which of them a reader should see first, which to keep for older viewers and which carry reservations.
body:
Start with Carl Theodor Dreyer's The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928). It is silent and built almost entirely from close-ups of bare faces, and Renée Falconetti's face is the film. The intertitles come from the trial record, and months of hearings feel like a single day. The climax is Joan's reception of the Eucharist from a compassionate priest, which agrees with the Church's rule that a penitent in danger of death is not refused absolution and Viaticum. Steven Greydanus finds some of the trial dialogue confusing but thinks older children can watch it. The riot in the square at the end is Dreyer's invention. Choose the Gaumont restoration.

Robert Bresson's The Trial of Joan of Arc (1962) is the best companion. It runs sixty-five minutes, uses only words from the trial and retrial documents, and has non-professionals speak them flatly. Florence Delay is remarkable for her stillness, and the film won the OCIC prize at Cannes. Time Out was hostile, and many viewers find it too austere to feel. Bresson's choice of what to keep is itself an interpretation, and the scenes of her last hours come from later testimony. Both films suit teenagers and adults better than children.

For a family, the choice is Victor Fleming's Joan of Arc (1948), with Ingrid Bergman. Take the restored 145-minute version, since the 100-minute release cut is confusing. The Technicolor won Oscars, and José Ferrer is a memorably slippery Dauphin. The first half is stiff pageantry, and critics from Bosley Crowther onward found it short on spiritual fire. The trial is much better, with Joan insisting that she is a prisoner of the English. The film opens with her canonisation and never doubts her mission. It makes Charles VII a villain who sells her for Burgundian money, whereas his counsellors arranged a truce and then made no effort to ransom her. Children of eight and over who can sit through a long historical drama will manage it.

Roberto Rossellini's Joan of Arc at the Stake (1954) films Claudel and Honegger's oratorio, with Bergman again as Joan. Phil Hall calls her performance extraordinary, though she was too old for the part. The film is static and theatrical, and the judges appear as animals, with Cauchon as a pig. That is Claudel's judgment on the court at Rouen and it does not mock the Church. It suits adults and older teenagers who already know the music.

Two silents show how the story was first told. Georges Méliès's Joan of Arc (1900) is ten minutes of hand-coloured tableaux, fit for any age, though a small child will need the story explained. Orléans has no siege and the trial shrinks to one interrogation. Antti Alanen places it at the head of the lavish Joan tradition. Cecil B. DeMille's Joan the Woman (1916) is in the grey area. DeMille invents an English lover whose betrayal causes her capture, and he frames the story with the trenches of the First World War, where Joan's ghost urges a soldier on a suicidal raid. The voices get brief and respectful treatment. Geraldine Farrar is uneven, and the spectacle is the reason to watch.

Three later films are also grey. Otto Preminger's Saint Joan (1957) adapts Shaw's play, with a script by Graham Greene. Shaw makes Joan a forerunner of Protestantism and nationalism, a private judgment set against the Church, and the film keeps much of that argument. Critics found Jean Seberg out of her depth, and Preminger later blamed himself. Jacques Rivette's Joan the Maid (1994) runs five and a half hours in two parts, with Sandrine Bonnaire as a believable country girl. Jonathan Rosenbaum calls it a plausible portrait of the teenage Joan. The reservation is its distance. It shows no visions or miracles, and the Church that later annulled the verdict and canonised her is absent.

The 1999 miniseries, with Leelee Sobieski and an Emmy-winning Peter O'Toole as Cauchon, is carried by its cast. It is grey because it will not commit on whether the voices came from God, and because it makes Cauchon Charles VII's own spiritual adviser, though he belonged to the English party throughout. Bruno Dumont's Jeannette (2017) sets Péguy's verse in a children's musical with metal music and headbanging nuns. Variety's Peter Debruge called it blasphemous, while Greydanus and Eve Tushnet find it playful and orthodox in substance. It is for adults and teenagers, and few will be neutral about it.

title: The life of Christ and the Passion on film
lead: Nine films on the Gospel story, from the silent Passion plays of 1903 to Gibson, and which to choose for children, for the family and for adults.
body:
For small children, begin with Pathé's The Life and Passion of Jesus Christ (1903). It runs about forty-four minutes in hand-coloured tableaux copied from Gustave Doré, and Steven Greydanus found it among the most accessible Jesus films for small children. There are no dialogue titles, so the viewer must already know the Gospel. It adds Veronica's veil, a pious tradition outside Scripture, and it goes on to the Resurrection and Ascension. Alice Guy's The Birth, the Life and the Death of Christ (1906) is Gaumont's answer, in twenty-five tableaux after James Tissot, with some three hundred extras. Historians single out a cut-in at Veronica and a pan following the climb to Golgotha, both unusual in 1906. Gwendolyn Audrey Foster criticises its casting of Black figures, apart from one of the Magi, in hostile roles. Both are suitable for all ages.

Sidney Olcott's From the Manger to the Cross (1912) is in the grey area. It was shot in Palestine and Egypt, so the Galilean hills are real, and the Holy Family passes the Sphinx on the flight into Egypt. But the film follows a Protestant reading of Scripture. It omits Christ's Baptism, it cuts Mary's request at Cana, and it ends at Calvary with John 3:16 and no Resurrection. Nothing in it contradicts the faith, but a Gospel film that stops at the Cross leaves the story unfinished. Greydanus pairs it with Pathé's film for the Resurrection and Ascension.

Cecil B. DeMille's The King of Kings (1927) opens as lurid Hollywood, with a half-dressed Magdalene, an orgy and zebras. Then the tone changes. H. B. Warner gives Christ dignity and gentleness, and the Last Supper is handled with reverence, as Peter holds the chalice to his heart and Judas crumbles the host and lets it fall. Greydanus calls the sensibility Protestant by default. The film makes Caiaphas a Roman appointee who pleads that he alone is guilty, to avoid blaming the Jewish people. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I, and children of eight and over can manage it with the intertitles read aloud.

Julien Duvivier's Golgotha (1935), the first sound film of the Passion, keeps Christ at a distance for its first half and lets us read him through Jean Gabin's tired Pilate, Harry Baur's Herod and Our Lady. Robert Le Vigan speaks only words from the Gospels. K. V. Turley calls it a cinematic icon for praying through Holy Week. Pilate is made more sympathetic than the Gospels require, and some viewers find the Jewish authorities stereotyped in the manner of 1930s European films. The crucifixion storm is frightening, so it suits children of twelve and over.

Pier Paolo Pasolini's The Gospel According to St. Matthew (1964) is the one to give an adult who wants the Gospel to speak. An atheist Marxist poet filmed Matthew almost word for word, with peasants for actors and southern Italy for Palestine. Greydanus gives it his highest artistic grade. It includes the charge to Peter, though it omits the genealogy and the Transfiguration. At 137 minutes in subtitled Italian it suits older children and up.

Two Hollywood films are grey. Nicholas Ray's King of Kings (1961) is reverent and handsome, but a Zealot revolt takes up much of its length, and Judas betrays Christ to force a rising. The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 rejects that motive. The Sanhedrin's part is reduced and Rome is made responsible, and the Legion of Decency gave it a Separate Classification for its poetic licence. George Stevens's The Greatest Story Ever Told (1965) presents Christ plainly as the divine Word, with Max von Sydow sovereign in the part and the raising of Lazarus set to Handel. Judas walks into the Temple fire, Lazarus is merged with the rich young man, and Satan appears as an invented hermit. Greydanus counts the Judas change the most damaging. Watch a long version, since the 1967 general release lost more than an hour.

Mel Gibson's The Passion of the Christ (2004) is for adults only. It is spoken in reconstructed Aramaic and Latin, and it cuts from the nailing at Calvary back to the Last Supper, which Greydanus ties to the Church's teaching that the Mass and the Cross are one sacrifice. Maia Morgenstern's Mary has almost no dialogue and gives the film its most affecting scene. Roger Ebert, who admired it, called it the most violent film he had ever seen. Much of the extra material comes from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, and the Resurrection lasts a few seconds. The portrayal of Caiaphas and the Temple crowd has been criticised, and the Roman Catechism puts the guilt on all sinners. A shorter Recut appeared in 2005.

title: Lourdes and St Bernadette on film
lead: Seven films on the Lourdes apparitions and the saint of Nevers, with advice on where to begin and which are still unreviewed.
body:
Start with Henry King's The Song of Bernadette (1943). Jennifer Jones won the Oscar for a performance built on stillness, and the black-and-white photography and Alfred Newman's score also won. At about two and a half hours it is slow, Lourdes is a Fox backlot, and Vincent Price's sneering prosecutor belongs in a melodrama. Steven Greydanus notes that the third act turns from marvels to the meaning of suffering, and that is its best stretch. The apparitions are treated as real but tested, and the Lady's words, "I am the Immaculate Conception", come four years after the dogma was defined. Franz Werfel's novel brings invented material with it. Antoine Nicolau becomes a devoted suitor, Peyramale is placed at a deathbed that came after his own death in 1877, and the prosecutor Dutour is made an anticlerical villain with an invented end. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I, and children of eight and over usually follow it well.

Jean Delannoy's Bernadette (1988) is a plainer chronicle and nearer to the documented girl. Shot around Lourdes, it never shows the Lady. The river noise drops away, a simple theme plays, and the camera stays on the witness. Greydanus credits fifteen-year-old Sydney Penny with spirit, even tartness, and her Bernadette answers doctors and clerics with disconcerting directness. The look is televisual and the English dub is awkward, though accounts conflict on whether each scene was in fact filmed twice, in French and in English. It suits a family audience.

Delannoy's sequel, The Passion of Bernadette (1990), covers her thirteen years at Nevers, with Penny again and Emmanuelle Riva as the suspicious superior. Few films about saints try to dramatise the long middle of a religious life, and this one does. Greydanus rates it below the first film because it is a sequence of convent episodes and has no story. Catholic News Service praised Penny's down-to-earth sanctity. One brief, graphic glimpse of an ulcerated breast during a medical procedure means parents should preview it for younger viewers. The original French with subtitles is better than the English dub.

Robert Darène's Bernadette of Lourdes (1961), titled Il suffit d'aimer in France, was scripted by the Catholic novelist Gilbert Cesbron. Neither the Lady's face nor her voice is given, and the film follows the Church's own sequence of caution, the question of her name and the answer. Stuart Galbraith IV finds its approach more poetic and less literal than the Hollywood film, and he lists its faults plainly. The budget was tight, people talk about events instead of showing them, the zoom lens is restless and the score is jaunty. The title, "It is enough to love", points to the Nevers years. The usual English version is dubbed and runs about ninety-four minutes. It is suitable for all ages.

Georges Rouquier's Lourdes and Its Miracles (1955) is a documentary in three parts. It follows the Medical Bureau's examination of cures, a pilgrim's day of devotions and two sick women filmed before and after their cures. Jean Collet judges it the most honest and affecting record of what happens at Lourdes during the pilgrimages. It lets the doctors' files and the pilgrims speak and does not hide the souvenir trade, and it presents the cures as facts the doctors could not explain, which comes close to the Church's own caution. It is hard to find and slow for young children.

Two films are in the grey area, both because nothing independent has been written about their treatment of the faith. Georges Pallu's silent The Wonderful Life of Bernadette (1929) runs ninety-six minutes and casts an actress as the Virgin, but no review exists and it is unclear whether a complete print survives. Jean Sagols's My Name Is Bernadette (2011) has Katia Miran as a determined, unsentimental girl, and she won a best-actress prize at the Mirabile Dictu festival. David Norgeot of Unidivers found the story thin and preferred Delannoy's two films. Nothing reported about it raises a doctrinal problem.

title: Fátima on film
lead: Seven films on the Fátima apparitions, from a 1928 melodrama to a 2009 independent film, with advice on which suit families and which are still unreviewed.
body:
Start with The 13th Day (2009), made by the illustrator brothers Ian and Dominic Higgins as Sister Lúcia's memory. It was shot cheaply on digital video, mostly in black and white with spots of colour, and its frames are composed like paintings. Steven Greydanus compares them to Vermeer and the austerity of Bresson, and he called it the best Fatima film, closer to the historical record than the 1952 Warner picture and more artful than Aparição. It gives the message in full, with the daily Rosary, penance for sinners, the vision of hell and the call to consecrate Russia. The six apparitions are condensed to four, the angel of 1916 is omitted, and Lúcia is played as reserved where the historical girl was outgoing. The vision of hell frightened one reader's children, so parents should preview it for under-tens.

Daniel Costelle's Apparitions at Fatima (1991) is the more literal film. Greydanus judges it the most faithful screen account, with dialogue taken from Lúcia's memoirs, and later called it the film to beat for fidelity, though not compelling art. It was shot at the Cova da Iria with a largely amateur cast, includes the angel's Communion to the children and speaks the second secret in full. The narration and music can intrude. It is in the grey area for its ending. After the deaths of Francisco and Jacinta, it closes on footage of John Paul II blessing the young cast at the premiere, so the story becomes a tribute to the post-conciliar papacy. A viewer can stop before the coda. The vision of hell and the children's severe penances may frighten the youngest.

For families, the choice lies between two 1950s films. John Brahm's The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima (1952), from Warner Bros., is well made and reverent toward the children and the Lady. Max Steiner's score was Oscar-nominated. But it recasts 1917 Portugal as a Cold War police state and adds the invented Hugo da Silva, played by Gilbert Roland, who takes over too much of the story. The angel apparitions are omitted, the children's detention is enlarged into a jail term among criminals, and the sun falls once instead of twice. Greydanus later called it more embellished than The 13th Day. Parents should explain the history first.

Rafael Gil's Our Lady of Fatima (1951) is the Spanish counterpart, and it was a major success. Gil shows the Virgin only in fragments, a mantle's hem, bare feet, light and a voice, and Inés Orsini plays Lúcia. Lúcia bears beatings and threats without complaint, and the furnace-room scene is intense, so younger children may be frightened. The administrator is turned into a Marxist plotter, which Aimaretti reads as aimed at Spain's Second Republic, and the lawyer Duarte is invented. The closing montage of later pilgrimages is the film's own addition.

Three further films are in the grey area because no independent review says how they treat the faith. The Day the Sun Danced (1988) is a short animation for young children from CCC of America, and it is unknown whether it includes the vision of hell or the request about Russia. Jorge Brum do Canto's Fátima, Terra de Fé! (1943) sets a sceptical doctor's conversion beside a staged account of the apparitions. The doctor and the cure are invented, and the Diário de Notícias presents the film as an example of the Estado Novo's official production. Rino Lupo's Miraculous Fátima (1928) is the oldest fiction feature on the subject, with footage of the 1927 pilgrimage and a screen debut by Manoel de Oliveira. Time Out Lisboa sums it up as melodrama, devotion and propaganda, and one summary says its story sets Fátima above Lourdes.

title: St Francis and St Clare on film
lead: Seven films on the Poverello and his first follower, from a 1911 short to Rossellini and Curtiz, with a view on where to begin.
body:
Start with Roberto Rossellini's The Flowers of St. Francis (1950), written with Fellini. It turns the Fioretti and the life of Brother Juniper into nine comic and tender episodes, played by friars from the Franciscan house at Nocera Inferiore. Nazario Gerardi plays Francis and Severino Pisacane plays Juniper, and their unaffected faces carry more conviction than actors could. Aldo Fabrizi is the one star, as a tyrant in absurd armour. Greydanus notes that Francis is the straight man and the brothers are the holy fools. Poverty here is freedom, obedience is literal, and the episodes do not add up to a plot. There is no conversion, no stigmata and no death, so a reader who wants the biography must look elsewhere. The 1952 American release cut episodes, so the Italian version is the one to see. It suits all ages, with the caution that it is subtitled and slow in the Italian manner, and Juniper is beaten and threatened with hanging.

Michael Curtiz's Francis of Assisi (1961) covers the life that Rossellini leaves out. It is the only Hollywood studio life of the saint, shot at Assisi with the cooperation of the Franciscans, and it takes in the conversion, the rule, Clare, the Sultan and the stigmata. Bradford Dillman, usually cast as a villain, plays Francis straight, and Dolores Hart is Clare. Critics found it respectful and inert, and A. H. Weiler compared it to tapestries hanging limp on castle walls. It invents Paolo, a friend and Clare's suitor, who carries much of the plot, and it turns Francis's aborted military venture into a papal campaign for Sicily when he had set out for Apulia. The Church is shown approving him through Innocent III and Cardinal Hugolino. It is more pageant than drama and suits the whole family, though children will find the speeches long.

Clare and Francis (2007) is a two-part Rai drama of about two hundred minutes that gives Clare equal weight. Mary Petruolo plays her as self-possessed from the start. Greydanus judged it a pick, finding the converted Francis joyful in humility and devoted to the Church, though he thought the drama weaker on Francis's worldly youth. Father Vincenzo Coli of the Sacro Convento praised it for avoiding the cliché of two little sweethearts, a romance for which there is no historical evidence. The early meetings and the families' dinner are invented. Children of eight or nine will follow it best one episode at a time.

Michele Soavi's St. Francis (2002), a Canale 5 television film of about three hours with Raoul Bova, is in the grey area. James Steffen of TCM found Bova lively and charismatic, preferred the film to Zeffirelli's Brother Sun, Sister Moon, and also found the style overwrought. The first hour is largely made up, including a childhood bond between Francis and Clare that the sources do not support. The reservation is the framing, which sets Francis's reverence for nature and the poor against a faith imposed by fear. Viewers should weigh how it treats the Church of his day.

Three silents complete the picture, and all are grey because no independent review describes how they handle the faith. Enrico Guazzoni's The Poor Man of Assisi (1911), the earliest film on Francis, runs twenty-four minutes with Emilio Ghione, and it was shot in Assisi itself. Mario Corsi and Ugo Falena's Brother Sun (1918) gives Clare an invented leading role in Francis's conversion, and her vision of the stigmata is also invented. Giulio Antamoro's The Passion of St. Francis (1927), made for the seventh centenary of his death from a story by Johannes Jørgensen, stages Francis as a second Christ. He is held like the dead Christ in a Pietà and returns to die riding a donkey. Clare's uncle Monaldo is an invented melodramatic villain. It is unclear whether a complete copy survives.

title: The Don Camillo films, in order
lead: Seven films follow Guareschi's fighting priest and his Communist mayor, from Duvivier's 1952 original to two later efforts that raise doubts.
body:
Start with the first film, The Little World of Don Camillo (1952). Julien Duvivier made it from Giovannino Guareschi's newspaper stories, and Fernandel as the hot-tempered priest and Gino Cervi as Peppone, the Communist mayor, fixed the pair for the whole series. By admissions it was the highest-grossing film of all time in both Italy and France. The crucifix over the altar speaks to Don Camillo in the voice of Christ and checks his temper; in one scene it tells him to throw away the stick he means to use. Fabrizio Valobra found the film fragmentary when it appeared, and the episodes are loose, but the talks with the crucifix give the comedy a moral centre. Children from eight will enjoy the slapstick. The sharpest moment is a suicide attempt by two young lovers, longer in the French cut.

The Return of Don Camillo (1953) is sadder. Roberto Chiesi calls it the more melancholy and bitter of the first two and rates its exile scenes the best in either, as the priest is sent to a mountain parish where the crucifix falls silent. Guareschi objected strongly to Duvivier's changes, and the French and Italian versions differ. Italian censors cut the most beautiful religious sequence, so look for the French print. A flood ends the film, and with it a dream of death that is the only real fright for young viewers.

Duvivier then withdrew, and Carmine Gallone directed Don Camillo's Last Round (1955), set in the general election of 7 June 1953. The Catholic film office's reviewer noted in 1955 that it repeats familiar situations. The best scenes are domestic, such as the giant priest drilling the mayor in arithmetic. A wartime story in which a priest crosses gunfire to hear a dying man's confession, and then refuses to repeat a word of it, rests on the seal of confession. Gallone also directed Don Camillo: Monsignor (1961), in which the promoted priest returns home from Rome with Peppone, now a senator. J. Grob, in Image et Son, was bored stiff, and at nearly two hours it is the slackest of the five. Fernandel's monsignor, embarrassed by his honour and itching to be a country priest again, is still a good comic idea, and the wedding quarrel has bite.

Don Camillo in Moscow (1965) is better than its reputation. Luigi Comencini made it to pay off a debt to Rizzoli and disliked it, and Jean A. Gili finds weariness in it. Yet the Russian half has a Mass in a hotel room, a secret visit to a dying woman and, best of all, a church turned granary where Christ speaks from the cross. It takes the Church behind the Iron Curtain seriously. Parents should know that Don Camillo lies about who he is and brushes off an oath as only a word, which the older moral teaching does not permit.

Two later films sit in the grey area. Don Camillo and the Youth of Today (1972) was made by Mario Camerini with Gastone Moschin and Lionel Stander after Fernandel's death. It satirises the post-conciliar Church from the side of tradition, with a bishop who wants the crucifix removed and a curate who would remake the liturgy, and it ends with a church wedding in the traditional rite. The reservation is that it is set inside the reformed Church, and it is unclear how far Don Camillo resists his bishop. It is also a weak film, and Gordiano Lupi finds the new leads shouting where Fernandel and Cervi were restrained.

The World of Don Camillo (1983) is Terence Hill's remake, and he directs himself in the title role. It keeps the talking crucifix and has Christ rebuke each of the priest's tricks. The reservation is the remake itself, which is glossy and thin, with a skydiving wedding, girls roller-skating in church and a priest who bribes, cheats and blackmails for laughs before Christ corrects him. The Filmtv.it reviewer called it a weak directing debut.

Watch the five Fernandel films in order if you can. The ending at the station in the 1955 film answers the farewell in the first.

title: Hollywood's priests
lead: From Going My Way to I Confess, seven Hollywood priest pictures compared for doctrine, craft and what children can watch.
body:
Begin with Going My Way (1944). Leo McCarey, who had a Catholic upbringing, made a comedy about two priests, and it is funny. Barry Fitzgerald's crotchety Father Fitzgibbon steals the picture from Bing Crosby's easygoing Father O'Malley, who takes over a debt-ridden parish without ever saying so. It won seven Academy Awards, Best Picture among them. It is long and loosely plotted, the opera interlude stops it dead, and the delinquents reform suspiciously fast. The parish is idealised and the plot runs on coincidence and a hit song. There is no coarse language, so it suits all ages, though young children may drift.

The Bells of St. Mary's (1945) is the better of McCarey's two priest pictures, thanks to Ingrid Bergman. Her Sister Benedict is strict, competitive, funny and devout, and Earley, writing in America in 1945, said that sisters at an advance screening recognised themselves in her. McCarey based her on his aunt, a sister of the Immaculate Heart community in Hollywood. The film is sentimental and long, and the Bogardus subplot is contrived, but the last scene in the chapel works. The New York Times found it too close to Going My Way. It was the highest-grossing American film of 1945 and carried a Legion of Decency A-I.

Boys Town (1938) puts Spencer Tracy in the cassock of Fr Edward Flanagan, the Omaha priest, and the performance won him an Oscar. Whitey, the bank robbery and the condemned man are invented, and Simcha Fisher finds that the second half slides into melodrama. It is in the grey area. It presents as an ideal a community where each boy worships as he pleases, and its motto that there is no bad boy leans towards treating sin as the product of circumstance. Fighting Father Dunne (1948) borrows heavily from it. Pat O'Brien plays the St Louis priest who opened a home for newsboys in 1906, and Variety praised him in 1948 for making the priest warm and human. The condemned-boy finale is melodrama, yet it gives weight to a priest's duty to a dying sinner. It is recommended without reservation and suits children old enough to take that ending.

Angels with Dirty Faces (1938) is the best made of the group. Michael Curtiz directs fast and hard, with Max Steiner's score, and Cagney makes the killer Rocky charming and lethal against Pat O'Brien's believable Father Connolly. The film is in the grey area. The Legion of Decency classed it B in 1938, and the glamour given to the gangster is the likeliest ground. Connolly also asks a condemned man to pretend to be a coward so that the boys will despise him, and Rocky goes to his death having refused the priest's ministry. Readers can weigh whether a pious deception and a death with no repentance shown make an acceptable ending. It is for teenagers and adults.

I Confess (1953) is the most Catholic film here. Alfred Hitchcock, raised a Catholic and taught by Jesuits, built a thriller around the seal of confession, and the film treats the rule as absolute. Montgomery Clift plays Father Logan almost entirely through silence and posture, and Robert Burks's photography makes Quebec's streets and churches part of the drama. Hitchcock thought it heavy-handed and humourless, and the flashbacks to Logan's romance are stiff. Jack Warner rejected the play's original ending, in which the priest is hanged before his innocence is proved. Few Hollywood films show a priest paying so high a price for keeping the seal. Teenagers and adults will follow it best.

The Keys of the Kingdom (1944) follows Gregory Peck, in his first Oscar nomination, as a Scottish missionary priest in China. Steven D. Greydanus calls it an edifying celebration of virtue in an imperfect hero, while James Agee came to find its sincerity bland. It is in the grey area. The Legion passed it for all audiences but flagged remarks open to a meaning not in accordance with Catholic doctrine. Chisholm asks as a student whether God values creed, which he calls an accident of birth, and he tells a mandarin that Methodist missionaries serve the same true God. The drift is towards indifferentism, and an adult should be ready to explain what the Church teaches. It runs 136 minutes and suits twelve and over.

title: Rome and the early martyrs
lead: Nine films set in imperial Rome compared, from the silent Quo Vadis of 1913 to Wyler's Ben-Hur, with the grey-area ones named.
body:
Start with Quo Vadis (1951). Mervyn LeRoy's MGM epic began the 1950s cycle of Roman spectacles and cost about $7 million, then the most expensive film ever made. Peter Ustinov's vain, petulant Nero steals it, and Leo Genn's ironic Petronius runs him close, while Robert Taylor and Deborah Kerr are stiff and the romance is the weakest part. What lifts it is that the Church stays central. Peter and Paul appear in person, the catacomb liturgy gets time, and the martyrs go to the lions singing. Lygia, Vinicius and Ursus are Sienkiewicz's inventions, the meeting on the Appian Way is a legend from the apocryphal Acts of Peter, and Nero's fall is compressed. The deaths happen mostly out of sight. It suits twelve and over, though three hours is a long sit.

Guazzoni's Quo Vadis? (1913) filmed the same novel and was the first great epic. It used some 5,000 extras and real Roman locations, and Wyke shows that scenes quote Gérôme's paintings of the martyrs. René Doumic found it stupefying. It is silent, with long titles, and its last shot of Christ breaking the chains of the faithful has no source in the book. Kawalerowicz's Quo Vadis (2001) is the most faithful version of the novel and the most expensive Polish film to that date. Ewa Skwara finds that it looks like the nineteenth century's idea of Rome, closer to Alma-Tadema than to modern scholarship, and Marek Zieleniewski thought it static and stagey. It is in the grey area, because Nero's feasts include bare-breasted dancers and the arena shows some gore, and a wordless closing image of Peter in modern Rome needs describing before one can judge it. It is for older teenagers and adults.

Fabiola (1949) is also in the grey area. Blasetti's huge postwar epic opened the wave of religious spectacles, and French critics in 1949 admired its handling of crowds, but it is very loosely drawn from Cardinal Wiseman's novel. The gladiator romance is invented, and the martyrdoms of Agnes, Pancratius and Tarcisius do not appear. The Italian Catholic film office classed it as for adults with reservations, and Vittorino Veronese of Catholic Action found its thesis questionable and its sensual scenes gratuitous. Manny Farber, seeing the shortened American cut, called it a chaos of disconnected sequences. Guazzoni's silent Fabiola (1918) is grey for a different reason. A print survives, but no independent review says what it shows of the martyrs or of Fabiola's conversion.

The Robe (1953) was the first CinemaScope film and won Oscars for its sets and costumes. Steven D. Greydanus praises the Roman prologue and Peter's account of his denial and forgiveness, and finds Richard Burton stiff and the conversion more a matter of special effects than of a changed life. It exaggerates the early Church's prominence in Rome and invents a clash with Caligula. Its virtues are reverence and clarity, and it carried a Legion of Decency A-I. Demetrius and the Gladiators (1954) continues the story, and contemporary critics liked it more than The Robe. Crowther enjoyed its mix of spectacle, action, sex and reverence. It is grey because Demetrius curses God, sacrifices to Isis and becomes Messalina's lover before Peter answers him with pity and he prays his way back. The film enjoys the sin it condemns, and an attempted gang rape and arena killings make it a film for fifteen and over. Michael Rennie's Peter is the best thing in it.

Ben-Hur (1959) is not a martyr film, though Christ stands at its edge. Judah and Messala are invented, and the meetings with Jesus are invented around the Gospel scenes. Greydanus says it does not transcend spectacle and melodrama but does both about as well as they could be done, and the chariot race remains one of the great action sequences. Crowther found Judah's meetings with Jesus dignified. At over three and a half hours, length is the test for children. The silent Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ (1925) is shorter by about an hour, and Greydanus rates its sea battle and chariot race at least equal. It is in the grey area. Christ is the frame of the story, and its faith is the general Christianity of Wallace's novel. The restored print also has brief nudity cut by censors in 1931.

title: Martyrs of persecution in modern times
lead: Nine films on the Church under the guillotine, the Mexican state, Nazi camps and Communist show trials, with Japan's martyrs of 1597.
body:
Begin with The Carmelites (1960). Bernanos wrote the dialogue about the sixteen Discalced Carmelites of Compiègne, who were guillotined in Paris on 17 July 1794 after offering their lives for peace and for the Church in France. The film keeps most of his plain, hard exchanges about fear and pride. Jeanne Moreau, Madeleine Renaud and Alida Valli lead a remarkable cast. Time Out found it static and pallid, and James Travers judged that it does justice to the play and that the scaffold sequence is overwhelming. The novice Blanche is fictional. The execution sequence is grim and shows nothing graphic, and the film holds teenagers better than small children.

The same Revolution produced the rising in the Vendée. Vaincre ou mourir (2023) follows Charette, the former naval officer shot at Nantes on 29 March 1796. Most notices were poor, and François Huzar found the battles illegible, but the religious side is sound, with Mass in hiding and a chaplain who refuses reprisals. It is in the grey area. The Puy du Fou made it, historians found it narrow and partisan, and the Republic's massacres are shown while the Vendéen killings at Machecoul are left out. Jean-Clément Martin also points out that Charette is shown signing a peace which only the Republican side signed. The War of the Vendée (2012) is a low-budget drama played by some 250 children and teenagers. Joseph Pearce, an editor for Ignatius Press, was charmed, while admitting it trades nuance for plain good against plain evil. It is grey because no independent review exists, and its source is Reynald Secher's disputed genocide thesis. It suits families with children of eight and over.

For Mexico, see The Fugitive (1947). John Ford's version of Greene's novel puts Henry Fonda's frightened priest in a state where religion is outlawed, and he walks back towards martyrdom. Steven D. Greydanus notes that Ford thought it his best, and Gabriel Figueroa's photography is its great strength. Dennis Schwartz found it turgid. The film makes the lieutenant the father of the priest's child and gives the priest only pride and fear, which softens Greene.

Japan's martyrs of 1597 come from an earlier age, but two films tell it. The 26 Martyrs of Japan (1931) was made by Japanese Catholics, and the Jesuit Hermann Heuvers co-wrote it. Goffredo Fofi praises Ikeda's command of late silent technique and faults the thin political background. Only about 65 minutes of a film originally some 150 minutes long survive. Philip of Jesus (1949) is grey because it fills the first Mexican-born saint's life with an invented double romance, and an hour of melodrama precedes a good ending.

Nazi and Communist persecution fill the rest. The Ninth Day (2004) lets a priest out of Dachau for nine days to persuade his bishop to collaborate. Greydanus gives it his top grade, and August Diehl's courteous Gestapo officer is more dangerous than a thug. The conversations are invented, since the real Jean Bernard left almost nothing about those days. Guilty of Treason (1950) dramatises the show trial of Cardinal Mindszenty, and Dennis Schwartz calls it cheaply made and over-moralising. Its value is as a document of its time. The Prisoner (1955) is better. Alec Guinness plays a cardinal broken without torture by an interrogator who turns his humility against him, and the cardinal and his country are fictional, a composite of the Mindszenty and Stepinac cases. The International Catholic Office for the Cinema gave it its Grand Prize for 1956, and it suits teenagers who can follow an argument.

title: Films for a family evening
lead: Eleven recommended films grouped by age, with the pace, the frights and the sad endings that parents ought to know first.
body:
Films rated for all ages come first. Rossellini's The Flowers of St. Francis (1950) tells nine episodes of the first friars, played by friars from Nocera Inferiore. It is gentle and often funny, though subtitled and slow, so younger children may need help with the pace. The Reluctant Saint (1962) is the better start for a mixed audience. Maximilian Schell plays Joseph of Cupertino, who flew, as slow, sweet and stubborn. Steven Greydanus admires how it holds back the miracles for over an hour, so that we meet Joseph as a person before he flies. Come to the Stable (1949) brings two French nuns to a Connecticut village to build a children's hospital with no money. Loretta Young and Celeste Holm play it with conviction, and the Christmas ending suits the season. Father Brown (1954) has Alec Guinness as Chesterton's mild priest chasing a thief across France, and the chase carries younger children through the slower talk. The Bells of St. Mary's (1945) has Ingrid Bergman as a strict, funny Sister Benedict, and nothing in it should trouble small children. Bernadette (1988) is a plain, slow account of the Lourdes apparitions, and Greydanus credits Sydney Penny with spirit, even tartness. Younger children may be upset by the officials who bully a sick girl.

The next group is for children of eight and over. The Miracle of Marcelino (1955) is the film to choose if you can only choose one. Pablito Calvo, aged six, gives one of cinema's most natural child performances, and the friars are warmly drawn. The ending is sad enough that younger children will want a parent beside them. The Little World of Don Camillo (1952) pairs Fernandel's priest with Gino Cervi's Communist mayor, and children enjoy the talking crucifix and the slapstick though the political jokes pass them by. The Trouble with Angels (1966) follows Hayley Mills as a prank-playing schoolgirl against Rosalind Russell's Mother Superior. Simcha Fisher would cut twenty minutes and notes a few gags that linger on schoolgirls' legs, but the film treats the convent as a way of life and Russell's grief at a sister's death is its best scene.

Two historical dramas suit older children best. The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima (1952) is a well-made Warner Bros. picture that takes the children's prayer seriously. It recasts 1917 Portugal as a Cold War police state, invents a lovable rogue, and has the sun fall once instead of twice, so parents should correct the history. Joan of Arc (1948) is long. Choose the restored 145-minute version, because the 100-minute cut is confusing. The first half is stiff pageantry, and the trial, where Bergman's Joan argues with her judges, is much better. The burning is shown without graphic detail.

Pick for the youngest child who will watch, and let the older ones put up with a gentler choice. Where a film is long, such as Joan of Arc or The Bells of St. Mary's, split it over two evenings.

title: The Passion on film
lead: From an 1898 New York rooftop to Gibson, which Passion films keep to the Gospels and which bend them.
body:
Start with Pier Paolo Pasolini's The Gospel According to St. Matthew (1964). The dialogue is Matthew's, cut and sometimes reordered but never rewritten, and the Passion is shown with little blood. Pasolini cast non-professionals and won the Catholic OCIC prize at Venice. Steven Greydanus gives it his highest artistic grade. It runs 137 minutes in subtitled Italian, so it suits older children and up.

Julien Duvivier's Golgotha (1935), the first sound film of the Passion, keeps Christ at a distance for its first half and lets us read him through the people around him. Robert Le Vigan speaks only words from the Gospels, and K. V. Turley of the National Catholic Register finds the method illuminating. Pilate is made more sympathetic than the Gospels require, and the Jewish authorities are costumed as stereotypes, in the manner of 1930s European films. The crucifixion storm may frighten children, and the film suits twelve and over.

Mel Gibson's The Passion of the Christ (2004) is spoken in reconstructed Aramaic and Latin. Its best idea is to cut from the nailing at Calvary back to the Last Supper, which Greydanus ties to the Church's teaching that the Mass and the Cross are one sacrifice. The reservations are serious. Much of the extra material comes from the private visions of Anne Catherine Emmerich, which are pious writing and no part of the deposit of faith. Mary Magdalene is identified with the woman taken in adultery, and Pilate is gentler than Philo and Josephus describe him. Roger Ebert, who admired it, called it the most violent film he had ever seen. Critics have also said that the priests and the crowd are drawn so as to revive the charge against the Jews as a people, and the Roman Catechism puts the guilt on sinners of every age. It is for adults only.

The silents show how the story was first told. Cecil B. DeMille's The King of Kings (1927) opens with an invented party at which Mary Magdalene is a courtesan, then settles into a reverent Passion with H. B. Warner as a gentle Christ and a Resurrection in colour. Cuts run from about 112 to 155 minutes. Alice Guy's The Birth, the Life and the Death of Christ (1906) stages the Gospel in 25 tableaux after Tissot in about 33 minutes, with a stylised, bloodless scourging, and suits all ages. Guy's Veronica wiping the face of Christ belongs to the Stations of the Cross and not to the Gospels.

The grey area begins with the earliest film. The Passion Play of Oberammergau (1898) was sold as a record of the Bavarian play, but it was shot on a New York rooftop from Salmi Morse's older San Francisco script and runs about twenty minutes. No independent review shows how it handles the Gospel. Sidney Olcott's From the Manger to the Cross (1912) was filmed in Palestine and Egypt and is reverent, but it reflects a Protestant reading, omits the Baptism, cuts Mary's request at Cana and ends at Calvary with no Resurrection. The Galilean (1921) films the Fassnacht family's Freiburg Passion play with more than 3,000 extras, and draws the priests of the Sanhedrin as hostile caricatures. I.N.R.I. (1923) frames the Gospel with a condemned Russian anarchist, makes Judas a disappointed revolutionary and stops at the Crucifixion.

The Martyr of Calvary (1952), with Enrique Rambal, is shown on Mexican television every Lent. Everything reported of it follows the Gospels, but only popular assessments exist, which is why it is grey.

Later films raise other questions. Nicholas Ray's King of Kings (1961) wraps the Passion in an invented Zealot revolt and has Judas betray Christ to provoke it. Philip Saville's The Gospel of John (2003) is word for word, but in the Good News Translation, whose "real food" in John 6:55 turns the passage away from a literal Eucharistic reading, as Greydanus notes. The Visual Bible: Matthew (1993) runs 265 minutes in the New International Version, another Protestant text.

Four films tell the Passion from its edges and are best kept until the Gospel is well known. Pontius Pilate (1962) follows the governor, played by Jean Marais, and suggests at the end that he believes, which the Gospels do not say. The Trial of Christ (1966) has Peter, Pilate and Barabbas recall the trial twenty-seven years later, so the Gospel account becomes one version among several. Trial of Jesus (1974), from Diego Fabbri's play, stages a mock trial in a Toledo synagogue, and one Spanish account says it sets the religious question aside. In Miracle of the Cowards (1962), people healed by Christ plot to free him from the cross, an invented story whose handling of the Crucifixion nobody has reviewed.

title: Mexican and Spanish religious cinema of the 1940s and 1950s
lead: Marcelino, Balarrasa, the Guadalupe films and lives of saints from two Catholic film industries, with the political and dramatic liberties each takes.
body:
Start with Ladislao Vajda's The Miracle of Marcelino (1955). A foundling raised by friars feeds bread and wine to the crucifix in the attic. Pablito Calvo gives a natural child's performance, and Christ is shown almost only through his hands, with the miracle signalled by changes of light. It is deliberately a tearjerker, and the ending is sad enough that small children will want a parent beside them. Choose the Spanish track, since the English dub on some US discs is poor.

Most of Spain's Catholic cinema in the early 1950s came from the director Rafael Gil and the writer-producer Vicente Escrivá. Their Our Lady of Fatima (1951) shows the Virgin only in fragments, a hem of mantle and bare feet, and ran for 56 weeks in a Madrid cinema. It also turns the official who detains the children into a Marxist plotter, an anachronism that one scholar reads as aimed at Spain's Second Republic. I Was a Parish Priest (1953) is the better drama. A young priest takes the miners' side in a bitter strike, with Claude Laydu, dubbed into Spanish, and Francisco Rabal. Rabal returns in The Cock Crow (1955), which moves Peter's denial to a priest under a Communist regime who disowns his priesthood, then confesses to his bishop and goes back. Escrivá also wrote Balarrasa (1951), directed by José Antonio Nieves Conde. Its reckless officer turned priest gives a moral fable a hard, noir-lit edge, though Fernando Fernán Gómez later thought the family's sins mild stand-ins for the real problems of the time. The last three suit teenagers better than young children.

Spain's saint films mostly follow their sources. Loyola, the Soldier Saint (1949) follows Ignatius's own Autobiography in the episodes that matter, though it invents an Infanta and a Roman sinner and carries the military patriotism of the 1940s. Teresa de Jesús (1962), with Aurora Bautista, follows Teresa's account of her trial by suspicious confessors, but opens with invented suitors and a duel, and her father did not send her to the convent the next morning. Fray Escoba (1961) keeps Martín de Porres at floor level among the broom, the infirmary and the begging round. René Muñoz won a special prize for it, and it is gentle enough for all ages.

Mexico's golden age made its own cycle. The Virgin of Guadalupe (La virgen morena, 1942) is the straightforward Guadalupe film. It came from a story by the Jesuit Fr Carlos M. de Heredia, a historian of the shrine, and opened with the endorsement of the Archbishop of Mexico. Its invented conquest plot puts a last battle between Spaniards and Aztecs in 1531, though Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Julio Bracho's The Saint Who Forged a Country (1942) has Ramón Novarro as Juan Diego and stages the apparitions reverently, but frames the whole as Fr Hidalgo's justification for the banner of the 1810 revolt. Hidalgo was excommunicated that year, and the film is grey for that reason. The Miracle Roses (1960) sets the apparitions against the conquest with Moctezuma, Cortés and Bishop Zumárraga. It is grey only because no review or Catholic rating describes it.

Bracho's Philip of Jesus (1949) ends well, with the martyrdom at Nagasaki and the fig-tree legend, but fills the hour before with an invented double romance and a prostitute double. It is grey and suits fifteen and over. Roberto Gavaldón's Ash Wednesday (1958), with María Félix and Arturo de Córdova, sets a priest serving secretly as a doctor in the Cristero persecution against a heroine whose hatred of the Church began with a priest's crime. It is for adults, and its treatment is known only from descriptions.

The lighter Spanish films pose smaller questions. Miracle of the White Suit (1956) follows a poor boy who will not make his First Communion without the suit his dying mother promised, and no review says whether the suit becomes the reward instead of the sacrament. The Song of Sister Maria (1952) is a singer's vocation story that ends with her death on the missions in India. It won state recognition, but her superiors' reaction when she saves their hospital with secret recordings has not been assessed. Berlanga's Miracles of Thursday (1957) began as a satire on a town that fakes an apparition for profit. The censors and a Dominican adviser added a pious fable in which St Dismas arrives in disguise, and it drew objections from traditionalists and progressives alike.

title: Convents and religious life on film
lead: Nuns on screen from The White Sister to The Nun's Story and after, sorting the sound portraits from the sentimental and the doubtful.
body:
Start with Fred Zinnemann's The Nun's Story (1959). No Hollywood film has shown the formation of a religious so carefully. The New York Times likened its first hour to a documentary, and the vows are explained through the words of superiors. Audrey Hepburn plays a Belgian surgeon's daughter who serves in the Congo and, after years of struggle with obedience, asks to be released. Edith Evans is formidable as a superior, and Peter Finch is the atheist doctor who calls her a "worldly nun". The second half loses the concentration of the first and the ending is hard, so it suits fifteen and over, with a parent ready to talk about vows. The order is not named and the story is fictionalised from Habets's life by way of Hulme's novel.

The older screen nuns are melodrama. In The White Sister, a noblewoman takes the veil believing her fiancé dead and keeps her vows when he returns. Henry King's 1923 version has Lillian Gish and Ronald Colman, and Bret Wood of TCM says seldom has Hollywood embraced the Church with so much passion. It ends with Giovanni's death, whereas the novel ends happily. Victor Fleming's 1933 remake moves the story to the First World War with Helen Hayes and Clark Gable. Mordaunt Hall thought it less real than King's film, and the earlier version is the one to choose.

For a family evening there are three studio comedies. The Bells of St. Mary's (1945) is the best, because Ingrid Bergman's Sister Benedict is strict, funny and devout, and a writer in America said that sisters at an advance screening recognised themselves in her. Come to the Stable (1949), with Loretta Young and Celeste Holm, is based on a real foundation that was a contemplative Benedictine monastery, which the film turns into an active order building a hospital. Greydanus calls it sweet and uplifting, though more sentimental than Lilies of the Field. The Trouble with Angels (1966), from Jane Trahey's memoir and directed by Ida Lupino, gives Rosalind Russell a dry, authoritative Mother Superior and Hayley Mills a vocation. Simcha Fisher notes that its sisters carry painful pasts. The slapstick has dated.

Robert Bresson's first feature, Angels of Sin (1943), sends a novice into a convent for former prisoners to save a hardened young woman and Doug Cummings praises how carefully it weighs her humility against her pride. It is in French and austere, and suits mature teenagers and adults. Le Dialogue des Carmélites (1960) keeps most of Bernanos's dialogue about fear and martyrdom, with Jeanne Moreau, Madeleine Renaud and Alida Valli. Time Out found it static, while James Travers called the scaffold sequence overwhelming. Blanche is fictional, though the Carmelites of Compiègne were not.

War brings the nuns into plotted stories. Conspiracy of Hearts (1960), with Lilli Palmer, has a convent smuggle Jewish children out of an internment camp. Time Out's David Parkinson called it a synthetic weepie. Douglas Sirk's Thunder on the Hill (1951) shuts Claudette Colbert's nursing sister in a flooded convent with a condemned woman, and her guilt and pride matter more than the mystery. John Huston's Heaven Knows, Mr. Allison (1957) strands Deborah Kerr's young nun with Robert Mitchum's Marine on a Pacific island. Greydanus observes that it understands the Marine Corps better than the convent. All three are fine for teenagers.

The grey area is wide. Marie's Story (2014) honours a teaching congregation before the Council, but its superior says dying sisters and priests only pretended to be glad to meet their Maker. Lilies of the Field (1963) is plainly Catholic, but its Baptist handyman is welcomed as sent by "the God of all faiths", and the exchange never runs the other way. The Singing Nun (1966) is a charming fiction in which a nun gives up fame for the missions. The real Jeanine Deckers did not, and she left the Church in 1967. The Miracle (1959) tells a Marian legend of a runaway postulant, but gives most of its two hours to her romances. Ida (2013) takes a novice's vocation seriously, yet its decisive episode is a night with a musician, and its ending can be read two ways. The Innocents (2016) honours the nuns' prayer, but its abbess abandons a newborn and a young sister kills herself, much of it invented. The Innocents is for adults and Ida for fifteen and over.

title: The apostles and the first Christians on film
lead: Peter, Paul, James and the Church of Acts on screen, from a faithful Lux Vide drama to Rossellini's austere series and Hollywood's invented heroes.
body:
Few films deal with the Acts of the Apostles, and the best of them rest on one performer. Start with Saint Peter (2005), a two-part Lux Vide drama with Omar Sharif as Peter. The Dove Foundation's Edwin Carpenter calls the performance compassionate and strong, and Stuart Dunn at CatholicMom notes how much of the first part's dialogue comes straight from Scripture. The second part is looser. It pads the Roman years with an invented gladiator and two young lovers, compresses the chronology, and has Paul executed before the fire although tradition places his death after it. Frequent violence puts it at twelve and over.

Andrew Hyatt's Paul, Apostle of Christ (2018) is a chamber drama set in Nero's Mamertine prison, where Luke, played by Jim Caviezel, visits Paul to record his memories. James Faulkner is a worn, combative Paul, and Greydanus finds Paul's remorse over the Christians he persecuted the film's most effective thread. The question it argues is whether a persecuted Church may answer Nero with force, and it says no. Scripture does place Luke with Paul in his last imprisonment, but the secret recording, the prefect and his daughter, and the armed faction are invented. Peter does not appear. The long dialogue scenes will lose younger children.

Roger Young's Paul the Apostle (2000) gives three hours to Saul's persecution of the Church, his conversion and the first Gentile mission, with Peter at the head of the Jerusalem community. Aldo Grasso of Corriere della Sera called the direction honest and expository. Peter Chattaway of Christianity Today thought it one of the weakest of its series, since invented characters such as the Sadducee Reuben and his wife take most of the time and Paul's own missions shrink to montages. It ends at Rome without his martyrdom. It is grey for proportion and for brief nudity, cut from a later US video, and it suits teenagers.

Roberto Rossellini's Acts of the Apostles (1969) is the strangest. Shot in Tunisia with largely non-professional actors, in long takes, it attends to how the first Christians ate, worked and prayed. Tag Gallagher sees in it the culmination of Rossellini's late historical work, and Jacques Siclier called it anti-dramatic. It is long and deliberately flat. It is grey because it removes the Ascension and almost all the miracles, and by Rossellini's own statements and Peter Brunette's reading it presents Christianity as a turning point in civilisation. A.D. (1985), made with Anthony Burgess, has Denis Quilley's Peter and Philip Sayer's Paul at its centre, and Arthur Unger found it a serious attempt. But a large share of its six hours goes to invented Jewish and Roman lovers, the vices of the Caesars and some arena violence, so it is grey and suits fifteen and over.

Santiago the Apostle (2017), with Julián Gil, follows James from his call to his martyrdom in AD 44 and the arrival of his body in Galicia. It is grey because no review exists, and a cast list with a sorcerer and a legendary queen suggests that the Compostela legend is told as fact.

Hollywood preferred invented heroes. Frank Borzage's The Big Fisherman (1959), with Howard Keel as Peter, spends most of nearly three hours on an Arabian plot from Lloyd C. Douglas, but its Gospel scenes, Peter's confession and commission above all, are given whole. Variety called it pious but plodding. The Silver Chalice (1954) invents a Greek silversmith commissioned to encase the cup of the Last Supper, and Paul Newman, in his first film, later called it the worst picture of the decade. Simon Magus dies through his own boast, where the apocryphal account has him fall at Peter's prayer. Take it as legend. Kevin Reynolds's Risen (2016) sends an invented Roman tribune to find the body after the Resurrection. Greydanus faults the Great Commission spoken without baptism in the Trinitarian formula, and a Mary Magdalene shown as a prostitute, but the bodily Resurrection and Ascension are affirmed.

Two films follow the robber freed in Christ's place. Richard Fleischer's Barabbas (1961), with Anthony Quinn, is brutal and intelligent, and Peter corrects the hero's error about the burning of Rome plainly. Alf Sjöberg's 1953 Swedish version, which Lagerkvist helped adapt, is likely closer to the novel's bleak spirit and is much harder to find. Neither gives a clear conversion, and both are for fifteen and over.

title: Missionaries on film
lead: From Spanish plague villages and the Congo to New France and Paraguay, which mission films honour the work and which turn it to other purposes.
body:
Start with Sáenz de Heredia's La mies es mucha (1949). A young Spanish priest, Fernando Fernán Gómez, pledges himself for his people's debts and serves them through a plague. A critic in Cristiandad in 1949 praised its restraint and its humour, and a Vincentian who had served at Cuttack advised on the village. The Indian setting was reconstructed with Spanish locations, and some Indian roles went to Spanish actors, so the picture of Indian society is simplified. It suits twelve and over.

Among the other recommended films, The Nun's Story (1959) includes the Congo and ends with a sister asking release from her vows, so it is for fifteen and over. The Left Hand of God (1955) has Humphrey Bogart pose as a dead priest at a Chinese mission and grow into the part. Bosley Crowther found it lacking credibility, and the Monthly Film Bulletin disliked its mock religiosity, but it keeps to the conditions of the Production Code. A Birth (2022), by Park Heung-sik, follows Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean priest, to his beheading in 1846. Park Ji-yoon of The Fact found it crammed with events, and Kim Jung-ki of Maeil Shinmun called it sincere. Cyril and Methodius (2013), a Czech and Slovak film, tells of the brothers' Slavonic liturgy and their quarrel with the Frankish bishops, adding a fictional double agent. Both of these suit twelve and over.

Two Hollywood films carry doctrinal warnings. In The Keys of the Kingdom (1944), Gregory Peck plays a Scottish priest who spends decades in China. It earned four Oscar nominations, and Crowther praised Peck's force. The Legion of Decency passed it but flagged statements open to a meaning not in accordance with Catholic doctrine. Chisholm tells a mandarin that Methodist missionaries serve the same true God, which drifts towards indifferentism. Leo McCarey's Satan Never Sleeps (1962) puts William Holden and Clifton Webb in Communist China. A. H. Weiler of the New York Times called it a lacklustre imitation of Going My Way, and its plot resolves a rape by marrying the victim to her attacker, so it is for adults.

Bruce Beresford's Black Robe (1991) takes a Jesuit of 1634 seriously on his own terms. It won six Genie awards, and Roger Ebert praised its realism but was depressed by the ending. Its reservation is that the priest's faith sits beside the Algonquins' dream-religion as near equals, and it contains sex scenes and graphic torture. Roland Joffé's The Mission (1986) has Jeremy Irons and Robert De Niro among the Guaraní, a procession of the Blessed Sacrament through gunfire, and Morricone's score. But it reverses history. The real Altamirano was a Jesuit sent by his own General, not a cardinal sent by the Pope, and the film honours a Jesuit who renounces his vow of obedience and leads an armed defence. Black Robe is for adults and The Mission for fifteen and over.

Two films on Francis Xavier are both grey for want of independent review. The 2006 Jesuit documentary, narrated by Liam Neeson, struck Video Librarian's Frank Swietek as more hagiography than history, and it dwells on accommodation to local custom. The 2022 Cristiana Video and EWTN docudrama is known only from the producers' notices.

Some mission films serve a state. Mision blanca (1946) is a Spanish melodrama set in Guinea, in which a priest finds that the cruel planter is his father. It fuses the faith with imperial nationalism, draws Africans as childlike, and has a missionary tear Our Lady's mantle to make a flag. Cardinal Messias (1939), on the Capuchin bishop Massaia in Ethiopia, was widely praised for Camillo Pilotto, but it was made in occupied Ethiopia and described by the Museo Nazionale del Cinema as a manifesto of the regime. Maurice Cloche's A Missionary (1955) is unusual in treating a young priest's disappointment at the slow work, but no independent review exists. Manoel de Oliveira's Word and Utopia (2000) lets the Jesuit António Vieira speak in his own words, but critics describe a freethinking priest persecuted by the Inquisition, and his trial turned on his prophecies of a Portuguese Fifth Empire. St. Patrick: The Irish Legend (2000) tells the core of his own story, but invents a corrupt British bishop and leaves Rome out.
